title: Running Scripts Through npm
learning_outcomes: Describe npm run and explain how it relates to Running Scripts Through npm.
Demonstrate Project-specific scripts in a small Node.js example and predict the observable result.
Test a failure, boundary, lifecycle, or version-compatibility case involving Passing command-line arguments.

content.intro: Running Scripts Through npm is part of getting started and working with the runtime. This lesson connects npm run, Project-specific scripts, Passing command-line arguments to a concrete Node.js example. Focus on the behavior you can observe, the assumptions the API makes, and one failure or boundary case.
content.why_it_matters: npm metadata and lockfiles make dependencies and project tasks repeatable across machines. Install from the lockfile in a clean checkout and run tests after dependency changes.

content_blocks.caption: Read the three labeled cards from left to right; the lesson steps connect the concept to a practical check.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: npm metadata and lockfiles make dependencies and project tasks repeatable across machines. Keep direct dependencies intentional, commit the lockfile, review lifecycle scripts, and audit updates.

items.title: npm run
items.text: npm metadata describes project scripts and dependencies; lockfiles improve repeatability but do not guarantee a dependency is safe.

items.title: Project-specific scripts
items.text: For Project-specific scripts, identify the relevant Node.js API or runtime behavior, trace its inputs and observable result, then test one invalid input, failure, lifecycle edge, or version-dependent assumption. Avoid inferring correctness from a happy-path run alone.

items.title: Passing command-line arguments
items.text: For Passing command-line arguments, identify the relevant Node.js API or runtime behavior, trace its inputs and observable result, then test one invalid input, failure, lifecycle edge, or version-dependent assumption. Avoid inferring correctness from a happy-path run alone.

items.title: Development and production scripts
items.text: Production readiness includes explicit configuration, health checks, observability, dependency management, and graceful shutdown; a local run alone does not verify deployment.

content_blocks.code:
const manifest = { scripts: { start: 'node src/main.mjs', test: 'node --test' } };
console.log(manifest.scripts.test);
content_blocks.run_instructions: Inspect this JavaScript in a local Node.js project. It is a static-validation teaching example: CodeLeaf does not run this arbitrary example in the API process. If it needs a package, file, server, database, or external service, provision that dependency in a separate local project and follow its official setup instructions. Run with `node example.mjs` when the example is self-contained, or adapt the required imports/inputs first.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Restore the starting snippet and inputs. Repeat with one different valid value and one invalid, missing, empty, or failure input appropriate to the example.

content_blocks.title: Guided example
content_blocks.text: Start with the code shown above. Predict the result before running it, then verify it against: node --test Change one input or simulate one failure and describe how the behavior should change. Install from the lockfile in a clean checkout and run tests after dependency changes.

content_blocks.title: Runtime and safety note
content_blocks.text: Teaching baseline: use a supported Node.js LTS release (Node.js 24 LTS as checked on 2026-10-13). The official releases page lists Node.js 26 as Current and Node.js 24/22 as LTS. Some advanced APIs, flags, permission behavior, embedded SQLite capabilities, module-loader hooks, and TypeScript integration are version-sensitive; verify the exact installed runtime. The Node.js 22 runtime available in the build-check environment is used only for syntax checks. This example is for learning and static validation, not for executing untrusted learner code inside CodeLeaf.

content.task: Create or inspect a small Node.js example for Running Scripts Through npm. Include at least one listed subtopic, document the expected result, and verify a normal case plus a boundary or failure case.
task_acceptance_criteria: The example demonstrates a named lesson concept, rather than only mentioning the title.
Expected output or observable behavior is documented and reproducible.
At least one invalid, empty, timeout, resource, or failure case is handled or explained.
The solution does not put secrets in source code and does not execute untrusted code inside the production API process.
hints: Start with npm run; identify the input, operation, and observable result.
Run the smallest relevant example in the selected Node.js release before adding frameworks or external services.
Test one failure or boundary case for Project-specific scripts, then explain why the outcome is expected.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating semver ranges or an audit report as a guarantee that a dependency is safe.
common_mistakes.why: The code may pass a simple demonstration yet fail with real inputs, resource limits, timing, or runtime differences.
common_mistakes.fix: Review provenance, release notes, transitive dependencies, and behavior before upgrading.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying a snippet without checking its runtime, dependencies, input assumptions, or cleanup behavior.
common_mistakes.why: Node.js APIs and surrounding ecosystem tools have explicit version, trust, and resource boundaries.
common_mistakes.fix: State the environment and dependency assumptions, then rerun the example from a clean starting state.
